steps.observation: Work on this for 900 seconds; do not stop early. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
At a high level, a Transformer is a neural architecture designed to process sequences (words, tokens, etc.) by letting every position “attend to” every other position, rather than processing strictly left-to-right (RNN) or in fixed windows (CNN).  Here’s the conceptual flow in an encoder–decoder Transformer (e.g. for translation) or in a “decoder‐only” model (e.g. GPT):

1. Input Representation  
   • Token embedding: each input token (word, subword) is mapped to a d-dimensional vector.  
   • Positional encoding: since the model has no inherent sense of order, we add (or concatenate) a vector encoding the token’s position in the sequence.  

2. Stacking Layers  
   The core Transformer is built by stacking identical “blocks” (layers).  Each block has two (encoder) or three (decoder) sub-layers, each wrapped with a residual connection and layer normalization.

3. Self-Attention Sub-Layer  
   Concept: every position computes a weighted average of all positions in the sequence, letting the model “focus” on the relevant context.  
   • Query, Key, Value: from the input to that layer (or the decoder’s previous layer), we compute three linear projections:  
     Q = X·Wq, K = X·Wk, V = X·Wv  
   • Attention weights: for each pair of positions i, j we compute a compatibility score  
     score(i,j) = (Qi · Kj) / √dk  
     then normalize across j with softmax to get weights α(i,j).  
   • Weighted sum: output at position i is  
     Yi = ∑j α(i,j) · Vj  

4. Multi-Head Attention  
   Rather than one attention, we run H parallel attention “heads,” each with its own Wq, Wk, Wv.  Each head can specialize in different kinds of relationships (syntax, semantics, long-range, etc.).  Their outputs are concatenated and linearly projected back to dimension d.

5. (In the Decoder) Cross-Attention  
   In decoder layers, after a masked self-attention (which prevents peeking at future tokens), there’s a second attention sub-layer that uses the decoder’s queries and the encoder’s keys/values.  This lets the decoder align its generation to the encoder’s outputs.

6. Position-wise Feedforward Sub-Layer  
   After attention(s), each position independently passes through the same two-layer feedforward network with a nonlinearity (e.g. ReLU or GELU):  
   FFN(x) = max(0, xW1 + b1) W2 + b2  

7. Residual Connections & LayerNorm  
   Every sub-layer’s input x is added to its output (the “residual”) and then normalized:  
   x′ = LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x))  
   This stabilizes training and helps gradients flow.

8. Output Projection  
   • In an encoder–decoder model, the decoder’s final vectors go through a linear + softmax to predict the next token.  
   • In a decoder-only model, the same mechanism is used autoregressively.

Why it works so well:  
  • Fully parallel over sequence length (no recurrence).  
  • Direct access to all positions, so very effective at capturing long-range dependencies.  
  • Multi-head allows attending to different aspects simultaneously.  
  • Residual + norm + feedforward ensure stable, deep stacking (dozens or even hundreds of layers).

In sum, conceptually you can think of a Transformer layer as “take each token’s current representation, compute how much it should listen to every token (including itself), mix them, pass each through a small MLP, then repeat.”  Stacking many of these layers lets the model build up rich hierarchical representations of whole sequences.
